1500.dq: Pitch accent in Japanese is fundamentally a word-level property, not a phrasal or sentence-level property, although it interacts non-trivially with sentence-level intonational patterns (Kawahara 2015 p.446).
1500.dloc: Kawahara 2015 pp. 445-448, 452-453, 480; Kubozono 2015 intro pp. 22-23; Sansom 1928
1500.prule: Lexical pitch accent (Tokyo Japanese): words contrast in presence vs. absence of accent and, if accented, in its location (n+1 patterns for n-syllable nouns); accent = HL fall in F0 after the accented mora; at most one accent per word (culminativity); prominence cued by pitch, not stress. No word-stress rule.
1500.srule: None: 'Japanese allows only one HL pitch fall within a word; this restriction – that there can maximally be one prominence within a word – is sometimes called “culminativity”' (p.452); Japanese is among the 'languages that do not possess stress' / 'non-stress languages' (p.480). No secondary stress or secondary/rhythmic accent is described.
1500.quote: The Tokyo dialect of Japanese exhibits lexical contrasts based on pitch accent; that is, there are minimal pairs of words that are identical segment-wise, but can be distinguished in terms of their pitch contours ... Japanese makes lexical contrasts in terms of pitch accent in two ways: (i) presence vs. absence, and (ii) if present, location. ... a. ame+ga (unaccented) 'candy+NOM' b. a'me+ga (accented) 'rain+NOM' ... 1500.tone: Word prosody is lexical pitch accent: 'word-level phonological prominence is signaled primarily by pitch (F0) rather than... duration, intensity and vowel quality' (Kubozono 2015 p.23); Kawahara p.480 calls Japanese a language 'that do[es] not possess stress' / 'non-stress language'; only two lexical tone levels (H, L), one HL fall per word; accented syllables are 'slightly longer than unaccented syllables (Hoequist 1982)' (Kawahara fn.1). 1501.prule: Primary stress on the word-final syllable; but if the final syllable is a suffix or a connective, stress falls on the penult (i.e. effectively stem-final stress). Epenthetic vowels in final clusters are always unstressed; lexical suffixes and the long-object numeral suffix -g̱n/-xn are always unstressed, while the numeral suffixes -daat, -on, -g̱aay carry primary stress. A listed set of ~106 words has lexical penultimate stress. No weight condition; stressed short vowels are often lengthened (stress conditions length, not the reverse).

1502.prule: Word-initial bisyllabic stress window, trochaic (default stress on syllable 1). A heavy (closed, CVC) second syllable attracts primary stress, but only if the first syllable's vowel is /ʌ/ (orthographic á); otherwise stress stays initial. Heavy syllables outside the window never attract primary stress.
1502.srule: In four-syllable words a second bisyllabic window (syllables 3-4) carries secondary stress; it is trochaic (default on syllable 3: ['i.si.ˌki.mo], ['ho.si.ˌne.lʌk]) and quantity-sensitive (['tu.tu.ˌwat.nʌ], ['ʌŋ.ŋʌ.ˌɾʌŋ.ŋʌ]); in two words a closed final syllable takes it although syllable 3 lacks [ʌ] (['pe.nde.li.ˌwoŋ], ['wi.ki.ni.ˌjoŋ]). Author: too few four-syllable words for firm conclusions. Trisyllabic examples carry no secondary stress; longer words are not discussed.

1505.tone: Banfield & Macintyre use 'accent' for tone (acute = high, grave = low, unmarked = mid; circumflex/inverted circumflex = falling/rising); minimal triplet be 'come'/'again'/'to blow'. 'Stress'/'emphasis' is explicitly a pedagogical approximation derived from tone height (highest-toned syllable of the word sounds most prominent), not an independent stress system. George 1970 (SAL 1(1)) treats Nupe purely as a contrastive-tone language (3 levels + 2 contours after Smith 1967) and says nothing about stress.

1509.dflt: Primary initial; no secondary in all-open trisyllables; secondary on alternate syllables in even-syllabled words (1,3 in four-syllable words) and on the 1st and 4th syllables in odd-syllabled words of five or more.
1509.prule: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable 'in the majority of words' (quantity-insensitive); non-initial primary stress in words with non-productive non-initial reduplication (stress on the first syllable of the reduplicated part) and in a listed set of words 'often where the stressed syllable has an initial liquid and is closed', for which 'it is not possible at present to formulate precise rules'; one minimal pair (gudurr 'sulk' vs gudurr 'pull tight') where stress may be contrastive.
1509.srule: Secondary stress (unaffixed words) is conditioned by syllable count and closed syllables: trisyllables with open 2nd and 3rd syllables have none; a closed 2nd or 3rd syllable puts secondary stress on the final syllable; four-syllable words stress the 1st and 3rd syllables, or the 1st and final if only the final is closed, or the 3rd if the 2nd is closed; in general an unstressed medial closed syllable must be followed by a stressed syllable and a final closed syllable attracts secondary stress; otherwise stress falls on alternate syllables in even-syllabled words and on the 1st and 4th in odd-syllabled words (all stated with 'it seems' hedges; words of 5+ syllables rare).

evidence_works.detail: A typological survey statement, not a study of Nyungwe: in §1 'Tonal contrasts' Hyman lists Nyungwe [N43] among 'the relatively few exceptions' to the Bantu binary H/L tonal contrast, in a 'discontinous band of languages starting in Mozambique with Sena [N44] and Nyungwe [N43], up around Lake Nyasa to Tumbuka [N21] and Nyakyusa [M31]... and finally the best known case, Swahili (G42)' (p. 162). No data, no Nyungwe-specific source and no statement on stress position accompany the claim; footnote 1 on the same page only thanks Gerard Philippson and two reviewers. The passage agrees with the entry's tone prose (Courtois 1900 treats no tone, only 'accento' and aspiration as distinctive) and supersedes its closing clause 'modern sources on its tone were not reached': a modern survey has now been reached and it lists Nyungwe among the few Bantu languages without a binary H/L tonal contrast.

1515.prule: One primary stress per word, placed by morpheme class: roots are lexically stress-retentive or stress-shifting; suffixes are inherently stressed, variable-stress, or unstressed; prefixes never stressed. Algorithm: stress the inherently stressed suffix closest to the root; else the root if stress-retentive; else (stress-shifting root) the variable-stress suffix closest to the root; else the root. Schwa is never stressed; unstressed root/suffix vowels usually delete.
1515.srule: Exists, placement not given: Mattina recognises a secondary degree of stress and says 'polysyllabic words sometimes contain a secondary stress', but states no rule for where it falls ('no systematic study of these phenomena has as yet been possible'). No stress rule is described; the words ストレス/強勢/stress do not occur in the 497-page grammar.

tn.translation: Kunigami has a pitch accent that distinguishes words by relative pitch height. ... The Kunigami accent kernel is realised exclusively by a pitch rise. ... we take Kunigami to be a system in which presence/absence and position of a raising kernel are distinctive. ... The kernel's position is the 1st, 2nd or 3rd mora from the end. So, based on presence or absence of a kernel and its position (1st, 2nd or 3rd from the end), four accent types are distinguished. ... Type a is kernel-less (unaccented); types b, c, d are kernel-bearing (accented). ... The prosodic unit bearing the kernel is the mora.

evidence_works.detail: Grammar sketch by the author of the 2017 dissertation the entry rests on, stated to revise it from later fieldwork (p.363: '本論文は，国頭方言の包括的な記述文法である横山（2017）を，その後の調査により修正し，より簡潔にまとめたものである'; main informant T.N, raised in Kunigami settlement). §4.3 (p.370) restates the same system: '国頭方言の名詞アクセントは，上げ核の有無と位置が弁別的な多型アクセントである。核を担う単位はモーラであり，アクセントが指定される単位は語である。' Data are citation forms in particle frames =nu, =kara, =kara=mu (tables 4-6), with kernel position argued from the b-type rightward shift before 2-mora particles. Refinements over 2017: (i) the raising unit is generalised, '上昇させる単位は，3 モーラ以下の語の場合は 1 モーラ，4 モーラ以上の語については 1 音節である' (p.370); (ii) for 4-mora words a fifth type is set up, '語末から 4 つ目に核があるため「e 型」と呼ぶことにする' (p.372), with very few members and an analysis the author flags as possibly problematic (p.373: '但し「ない要素」に核が移動すると考えることは問題があるかもしれない…この型には非常に少数の語が所属する'); (iii) 2017's 4-mora d-type words (kiNnjuu, jumudui) are reanalysed as c-type plus a leftward kernel shift off the first mora of a heavy syllable (fn.4, p.372: '横山（2017）では，これらの語を d 型に分類したが，ここ記述する理由で解釈を変更した'). No instrumental measurement; pitch given as impressionistic H/L transcription.

1517.prule: In the Baxter-Sagart reconstruction a word (root) is at most a minor presyllable (*C- or *Cə-, 'preinitial') plus one major syllable; the major syllable is stressed and any minor syllable unstressed, giving disyllabic (sesquisyllabic) words an iambic weak-STRONG rhythm, i.e. stress on the final = major = full-vowel syllable; monosyllabic words are a single stressed major syllable. No tones.

1518.prule: Stress on the root syllable of the word (inherited Germanic accent shift 'to the ROOT syllable in ALL cases'); all nonroot (stem-formant, inflectional) syllables are unstressed/weakly stressed. In the unprefixed lexicon of the older runic corpus the root syllable is the word-initial syllable. Weight plays no role in stress placement (weight/length of the root conditions later syncope of the following unstressed vowel, not stress position).

1519.dq: It is not necessary to mark the stress of Old French words, for the primary stress may be placed by an inviolable rule — on the ultima unless the ultima vowel be e̥, in that case on the penult

1519.heavy: Any syllable whose vowel is not the feminine e (e̥); a final syllable with e̥ cannot bear the primary stress.
1519.dflt: Penult, by the letter of the rule (exhaustive two-way rule: ultima, else penult whenever the ultima vowel is e̥, whatever the penult holds). The all-reduced window does not arise: sec. 265 'In the ultima only e̥ is to be found unstressed', sec. 264 'There are no unstressed penult vowels in the second Old French period' (no proparoxytones), so the penult of an e̥-final word is always the tonic, full-vowel syllable.
1519.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable (ultima), unless the vowel of the ultima is the feminine e (e̥, schwa-like reflex of Latin final -a / support vowel), in which case stress falls on the penult. Stated as an 'inviolable rule'.

tn.quote: 15 th century West Frisian developed the possibility of having those two stress markers on different syllables, independent of the quality of the second syllable. 1522.dq: In all uncompounded words the chief stress falls upon the stem-syllable and always remains there even when suffixes and inflexional endings follow it. This syllable is always the first of the word.

1522.prule: Chief stress on the stem (root) syllable; in ALL uncompounded words this is the first syllable of the word and it stays there regardless of suffixes and inflexional endings (Wright 1906 sec. 12) -- fixed word-initial, quantity-insensitive, no hedge. Separate compound rule (morphological): stress on the stem syllable of the FIRST member if the second member is a noun or adjective (nominal prefixes stressed: Braune urteil, urcundo, antlaz, antwurti), on the stem syllable of the SECOND member if it is a verb or deverbal (verbal prefixes gi-, fir-, bi-, int-, ir-/ar-, zi- proclitic and unstressed). = Germanic root stress.
1522.srule: Wright sec. 12 states no secondary stress. Braune 1891 sec. 63 states a nebenton (secondary stress) on heavy medial syllables -- derivational syllables that are long-vowelled or closed by consonant clusters (-ari, -inn-, -ig, -in, -isc, -ing/-ling, -oht, -oro/-osto, -od/-oti, -unga, the e/o of weak verbs III/II) -- and (Anm. 2) a strong nebenton on the stem syllable of the second member of compounds; this secondary stress is weight- and morphology-conditioned, not a quantity-insensitive position, so it is not marked in the rule string.

evidence_works.detail: Not instrumental. Allen argues the accent's placement and nature from vowel weakening/syncope (aetas, pergo, confectus < confactus), from syllable quantity (re-lic-tus accented like re-la-tus), from ictus/accent agreement in the hexameter and from iambic shortening, and restates the ancient grammarians (Quintilian i.5.30, Servius, Pompeius, Varro) for the rule itself. On the Old-Latin stage the record is keyed to, Allen agrees with Lindsay 1915: prehistoric stress on the first syllable, and 'There may perhaps be a survival of this initial accent in the senarius in such forms as facilia, cecidero, though this is disputed' (p. 83).

1526.prule: Primary word accent falls on the same syllable as in Vulgar Latin, i.e. it continues the Classical Latin quantity-determined accent; after Old Provençal vowel losses this yields final stress (bontát, requér, filhóls, lai) or penultimate stress (cónte, cadéira, téngra) depending on the etymon, so position is lexically (etymologically) given, not computable from syllable count; no synchronic weight rule is stated.
1526.srule: None described for Old Provençal words. Grandgent treats the secondary accent only historically: the Vulgar Latin secondary accent (on the second syllable from the primary: cógitó, cupìditátem) lasted into Provençal until the intertonic vowel dropped; then 'the secondary stress, being brought next to the primary, disappeared, and its vowel was henceforth unaccented' (cupĭdĭtātem > cobeitát). No synchronic secondary or rhythmic stress rule is given.

dfl.q: In general, Occitan words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable: ... cantar ‘to sing,’ partir ‘to leave’ ... Words ending in a vowel are stressed on the penult, or next-to-final syllable ... canta ‘he sings’ ... paire ‘father,’ glazi ‘sword’ The position of stress in Occitan almost always corresponds to the CL etymon or its reflexes in other Romance languages (cf. ch. 11).
